claim: Nitrogenase is the only known enzyme family that catalyzes the reduction of atmospheric dinitrogen (N2) to ammonia (NH3).
source: Nitrogenase provides access to bioessential nitrogen via the reduction of highly inert atmospheric dinitrogen (N2) to ammonia (NH3) (Rucker and Kaçar, 2024). In select microbes called diazotrophs, this pathway is exclusively performed by members of the nitrogenase metalloenzyme family that catalyze the cleavage of the strong N≡N bond.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rucker and Kaçar, 2024, and is stated as an exclusive pathway performed by nitrogenase.

claim: Biological nitrogen fixation existed more than 3 billion years ago.
source: Age-calibrated, phylogenomic analyses of nitrogenase genes (Parsons et al., 2021) and nitrogen isotopic signatures preserved in the geologic record (Stüeken et al., 2015) both provide evidence for the existence of biological nitrogen fixation more than 3 billion years ago.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to phylogenomic analyses (Parsons et al., 2021) and nitrogen isotopic signatures (Stüeken et al., 2015).

claim: Nitrogenases are extremely sensitive to oxygen, which degrades the bound metalloclusters required for their enzymatic activity.
source: Notably, nitrogenases are extremely sensitive to oxygen, which degrades the bound metalloclusters required for their enzymatic activity and multimeric structure (Robson and Postgate, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Robson and Postgate, 1980.

claim: Nitrogenases originated in anaerobic organisms inhabiting an anoxic planet more than 3.2 billion years ago.
source: Nevertheless, these enzymes, which originated in anaerobic organisms inhabiting an anoxic planet >3.2 billion years ago (Stüeken et al., 2015), evolved through the progressive oxygenation of Earth's surface environment (beginning ~2.4–3 billion years ago) (Lyons et al., 2024; Lyons et al., 2014) and genetic acquisition by aerobic organisms (Boyd et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stüeken et al., 2015, Lyons et al., 2024, Lyons et al., 2014, and Boyd et al., 2015.

claim: Earth's surface environment underwent progressive oxygenation beginning approximately 2.4–3 billion years ago.
source: Nevertheless, these enzymes, which originated in anaerobic organisms inhabiting an anoxic planet >3.2 billion years ago (Stüeken et al., 2015), evolved through the progressive oxygenation of Earth's surface environment (beginning ~2.4–3 billion years ago) (Lyons et al., 2024; Lyons et al., 2014) and genetic acquisition by aerobic organisms (Boyd et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lyons et al., 2024 and Lyons et al., 2014.

claim: This study generated 5378 protein structures, representing a more than threefold increase compared to available nitrogenase structures in the PDB.
source: We began our structural investigation of nitrogenase evolutionary history by conducting a large-scale structure prediction analysis, encompassing 5378 protein structures, a more than threefold increase compared to available nitrogenase structures in the PDB.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and refers to the number of structures generated in this study.

claim: The nitrogenase phylogenetic dataset includes five major clades: Nif-I, Nif-II, Nif-III, Vnf, and Anf.
source: The topology of the nitrogenase phylogenetic dataset Garcia et al., 2023 used in the present study reveals five major clades: Nif-I, Nif-II, Nif-III, Vnf, and Anf (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the phylogenetic tree with labeled clades.

claim: Vnf and Anf homologs are nested within the Nif-III clade.
source: Both Vnf and Anf homologs are nested within the Nif-III clade.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the phylogenetic relationships.

claim: All nitrogenase structures were predicted with high confidence, with pLDDT scores ranging between approximately 82 and 98.
source: We found that all nitrogenase structures were predicted with high confidence, assessed by the predicted Local Distance Difference Test (pLDDT) (Jumper et al., 2021; Mariani et al., 2013). pLDDT scores ranged between ~82 and 98 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Confidence was lowest for H-subunit structures (median pLDDT ≈ 88) and highest for K-subunit structures (median pLDDT ≈ 98).
source: Within this range, confidence was lowest for H-subunit structures (median pLDDT ≈ 88) and highest for K-subunit structures (median pLDDT ≈ 98).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific median pLDDT values for different subunits.

claim: Predicted nitrogenase structures have sufficient variations to resolve phylogenetic relationships.
source: We observe that predicted nitrogenase structures have sufficient variations to resolve phylogenetic relationships.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by subsequent analysis of structural variation.

claim: Overall structural differences between nitrogenases are small, with RMSD values less than 3 Å.
source: Although in this case, this metric indicates overall small differences (<3 Å) (Figure 2A), it still strongly correlates with sequence identity (Figure 2B), indicating that even minor structural variations can recapitulate sequence-based phylogenetic distinctions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RMSD strongly correlates with sequence identity in nitrogenase structures.
source: Although in this case, this metric indicates overall small differences (<3 Å) (Figure 2A), it still strongly correlates with sequence identity (Figure 2B), indicating that even minor structural variations can recapitulate sequence-based phylogenetic distinctions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B showing the correlation.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of nitrogenase structures by pairwise RMSD largely reproduces the major clades.
source: Hierarchical clustering of nitrogenase structures by pairwise RMSD largely reproduces the major clades (Nif-I, Nif-II, Nif-III, Vnf/Anf) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C showing the hierarchical clustering.

claim: Three insertion events distinguish nitrogenase variants: a D-subunit C-terminus extension unique to Anf, a K-subunit N-terminus extension unique to Nif-I, and a D-subunit insertion unique to Nif-II.
source: The structural predictions identified three insertion events that distinguish nitrogenase variants. These insertions likely contribute significantly to the phylogenetic signal encoded within structural features (Figure 3A): a D-subunit C-terminus extension (~60 residues) unique to Anf (Figure 3B), a K-subunit N-terminus extension (~8–40 residues) unique to Nif-I (Figure 3C), and a D-subunit insertion (~55 residues) unique to Nif-II (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 3A-D showing the insertions.

claim: The K-subunit N-terminus extension evolved progressively in length through several deep-time ancestors of the Nif-I clade.
source: By contrast, we observed that the K-subunit N-terminus insertion evolved progressively in length (Figure 3B and D) through several deep-time ancestors of the Nif-I clade (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 3B, 3C, and 3D.

claim: All insertions are exposed at the surface of the DDKK protein complex.
source: First, all insertions are exposed at the surface of the DDKK protein complex (Figure 3B–D), and all comprise varying proportions of helix or loop regions in both extant and ancestral structures.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 3B-D showing the structural locations.

claim: No major deletion events were detected in the evolutionary history of nitrogenase.
source: As a side observation, our analysis detected no major deletion events in the evolutionary history of nitrogenase.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: Total surface area is greatest in the Nif-II clade.
source: For example, total surface area (summed over each protein subunit in the DDKK complex) is distinct between Nif-I, Nif-II, and Nif-III/Vnf/Anf, and greatest in the Nif-II clade (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nif-I homologs have the largest number of intersubunit molecular contacts and intersubunit binding affinities.
source: Nif-I homologs (and particularly those with longer K-subunit extensions) have the largest number of intersubunit molecular contacts and intersubunit binding affinities, as calculated with Prodigy (Vangone and Bonvin, 2015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4—figure supplement 1C and 4B.

claim: Nif-III nitrogenases have the least number of intersubunit contacts and weakest binding affinities.
source: By contrast, homologs with the least number of intersubunit contacts and weakest binding affinities are Nif-III nitrogenases, which notably contain none of the described insertions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text as a contrast to Nif-I homologs.

claim: The proportion of charged residues across DDKK proteins correlates with ancestor age.
source: The only structural attribute that we found correlated with ancestor age was the proportion of charged residues across DDKK proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E). Accordingly, we observed a weak negative correlation between phylogenetic distance from the root and proportion of charged residues (Spearman R ≈ –0.261).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text with a specific Spearman correlation coefficient and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Three ancestral nitrogenase variants were crystallized: Anc1A, Anc1B, and Anc2.
source: Three previously characterized ancestral variants were targeted from phylogenetic nodes within the evolutionary lineage of Azotobacter vinelandii Nif (wild-type, 'WT') (Figure 5A; Garcia et al., 2023): Anc1A, Anc1B, and Anc2.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A showing the phylogenetic positions.

claim: Anc1A and Anc1B are the same age, whereas Anc2 is reconstructed from an older phylogenetic node.
source: Anc1A and Anc1B are the same age, whereas Anc2 is reconstructed from an older phylogenetic node.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the ancestral variants.

claim: An estimated maximum age of approximately 2.5 billion years for Group I nitrogenases is inferred from the timing of the GOE.
source: An estimated maximum age of approximately 2.5 billion years for Group I nitrogenases—and consequently for Anc1 and Anc2—is inferred from the timing of the GOE (Garcia et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations to Garcia et al., 2023 and Lyons et al., 2014.

claim: Ancestral nitrogenases required different conditions for crystallization relative to modern proteins, specifically pH 6.5.
source: We found that ancestral nitrogenases required different conditions for crystallization relative to that required for modern proteins. Specifically, all ancestors crystallized at pH 6.5, which is unusually acidic for nitrogenase (Peters et al., 1997; Spatzal et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations to Peters et al., 1997 and Spatzal et al., 2011.

claim: All ancestral proteins crystallized in space group P 212121, which differs from the space groups for the same proteins in A. vinelandii NifDK, C. pasteurianum Nif, and K. pneumoniae NifDK.
source: In addition, all ancestral proteins crystallized in space group P 212121, which differs from the space groups for the same proteins in A. vinelandii NifDK (i.e., WT; space group P 21), Clostridium pasteurianum Nif (space group P 21), and Klebsiella pneumoniae NifDK (space group C 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text with specific space group identifications.

claim: Global structural differences between the ancestors and WT A. vinelandii DDKK are relatively minor and within the range of variation for available extant structures.
source: Global structural differences between the ancestors and WT A. vinelandii DDKK are relatively minor and within the range of variation for available extant structures.

claim: The RMSD between Anc2 and WT (0.24 Å) is smaller than that between Anc1A and WT (0.31 Å).

claim: Predictions for nitrogenase variants had high similarity (average RMSD <1.4 Å) to experimentally determined structures.

evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A showing the comparison.
